item.title: Qatar’s $5.5 million startup fund could open doors for African founders
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel Nwosu
item.description: Qatar is offering foreign tech startups up to $5.5 million in funding, alongside residency and relocation support, as it seeks to attract entrepreneurs to Doha. African founders could benefit from the programme, but accessing the funding comes with conditions, and Qatar's startup ecosystem is still developing.
item.content:encoded:
Qatar is offering foreign tech founders up to $5.5 million in funding to back growth-stage startups that want to operate in the gas-rich Gulf country, alongside visas, subsidised housing, and business support. Behind the incentives is a broader ambition to make Qatar a destination for global entrepreneurs.

For a tech founder considering where to build their next company, Qatar is making an unusual offer: move your business to the Gulf state, and receive up to $5.5 million in investment funding, help securing residency, subsidised office space, and housing support.

The offer, open to founders globally, including those from Africa, comes through the Startup Qatar Investment Programme, an initiative run by the government-owned Qatar Development Bank (QDB) to attract foreign entrepreneurs looking to establish or expand their businesses in the country.

item.title: Why the UK is becoming a base for African tech companies
item.dc:creator: Opeyemi Kareem
item.description: A November 2026 report by TLP Advisory reveals that the UK is a key base for African tech companies.
item.content:encoded:
In March 2026, the United Kingdom government published a list of Nigerian companies expanding operations in the UK, including fintechs Moniepoint, Kuda and LemFi. Their expansion reflects a growing interest among African tech companies in the UK as a base for building and growing their businesses.

A November 2026 report by TLP Advisory, a cross-border venture law firm, examined 100 technology companies across Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, Egypt, Ghana and Morocco that have documented affiliations in the UK, the United States and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The US was the most common destination, with 67% of the companies affiliated there. The UK followed at 32%, while 23% were connected to the UAE.

item.title: Kenya’s WayaWaya partners with Choice Bank to launch AI-powered banking services
item.dc:creator: Opeyemi Kareem
item.description: WayaWaya has partnered with Choice Bank to launch banking services to bring more banking capabilities to its AI-powered financial services platform.
item.content:encoded:
WayaWaya, a Kenyan company building AI-powered financial services for banks and merchants, has partnered with microfinance bank Choice Bank to expand its platform with banking services.

The service, WayaWaya Banking, will allow customers to open bank accounts, hold funds in multiple currencies, make local and international transfers, and pay utilities through a platform regulated by the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK). Under the partnership, Choice Bank will provide the regulated banking infrastructure, while WayaWaya will build the technology and manage the customer experience.

item.title: Nigeria is rewriting its cyber laws, but can it secure its systems against hackers?
item.dc:creator: Progress Godfrey
item.description: Nigeria is reviewing its cybersecurity laws to counter mounting threats as artificial intelligence (AI) makes fraud, digital deception, and attacks on critical infrastructure harder to detect.
item.content:encoded:
Nigeria is reviewing its cybersecurity laws to counter mounting threats as artificial intelligence (AI) makes fraud, digital deception, and attacks on critical infrastructure harder to detect.

AI was linked to 55% of cybercrime incidents recorded across Africa last year, while deepfake cases increased sevenfold between the second and fourth quarters of 2024. Cybercriminals are using AI to automate scams, create convincing fake identities, and more quickly identify weaknesses in critical systems. This means attackers are adopting the technology faster than institutions can strengthen their defences, leaving existing security systems and laws struggling to keep up. 

This growing technology gap is the primary driver behind the current legislative review, as the Nigerian government acknowledges that existing frameworks fail to provide adequate guardrails or align with international best practices.

item.title: OPay was used to scaling regulatory walls until its IPO
item.dc:creator: Muktar Oladunmade
item.description: If OPay is to succeed on its second IPO attempt, it will need to revisit how well it bounced back from inquiries by Nigerian policymakers.
item.content:encoded:
OPay’s rise to one of Nigeria’s largest fintechs came after a series of regulatory hurdles. Now, the latest—an inquiry from Chinese regulators—led it to withdraw its $304 million New York listing on October 30. How the company handled the earlier hurdles best guides what it might do now.

Last week, as OPay’s executives rang the opening bell at the New York Stock Exchange, it was supposed to symbolise the final step in the company’s long journey from a small mobile money operator in Nigeria to a global fintech.

Instead, it was another in a long series of hurdles the fintech has endured as the company suspended the listing after a regulatory inquiry from China, its founder Zhou Yahui’s home country.

Since Opera, the browser company owned by a consortium led by Zhou, acquired a controlling stake in Paycom, a mobile-money operator, in 2018, a mix of luck, almost endless capital, and a willingness to start afresh has created a fintech with 50 million users.

item.title: Massive wants to help small businesses turn Google searches into customers
item.dc:creator: John Adoyi
item.description: Massive combines automated optimisation with human account managers who monitor search rankings and review business profiles.
item.content:encoded:
For four years, Segun Olaiya worked in local search engine optimisation (SEO) in the United States, helping large operations, including AT&T and businesses in San Diego and Texas, improve their visibility in online searches.

But he observed that marketing technology largely catered to organisations with multiple locations, leaving smaller businesses overlooked.

“Most of this kind of industry, which is marketing technology, is usually focused around big organisations that have multiple locations across cities and states that want to be as visible as possible. But small businesses are not always really paid attention to,” Olaiya told TechCabal in an interview.

He began helping small business owners manually optimise their Google Business Profiles. Some reported receiving more calls from customers who found them through organic search rather than paid advertisements. “They were like, ‘Oh, now I get more calls,’” he recalled.

item.title: Optasia wants to move beyond airtime credit as microfinance drives growth
item.dc:creator: Phathisani Moyo
item.description: Optasia is moving beyond airtime advances into AI-powered microfinance, targeting consumers and small businesses underserved by traditional lenders as it expands its digital lending business.
item.content:encoded:
One year after its R23.5 billion ($1.4 billion) debut on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE), Africa’s biggest securities market, Optasia is growing faster than expected. But its biggest opportunity may lie beyond the airtime advances that built its business.

The pan-African-listed fintech generated $270 million in revenue in the first nine months of 2026, up 45% year on year, as it accelerated its shift towards microfinance. The business uses artificial intelligence (AI) and alternative data to extend credit to underserved consumers. It now wants more than 80% of its revenue to come from microfinance solutions.

item.title: Nigeria’s Central Bank wants every crypto P2P payment linked to a bank transaction
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel Nwosu
item.description: The new rules underscore the CBN’s push to tighten its grip on crypto trading, giving the regulator greater visibility into who moves money through P2P platforms.
item.content:encoded:
Nigeria’s Central Bank has introduced new rules requiring cryptocurrency peer-to-peer (P2P) platforms to link every digital asset transaction to its corresponding bank payments, tightening oversight of how Nigerians trade cryptocurrencies outside traditional exchanges.

Under the regulations, P2P operators must route naira payments through banking or CBN-approved payment channels, verify traders’ identities, and keep records connecting each payment to the corresponding cryptocurrency transfer.

The requirements are part of the CBN’s new framework for non-security virtual assets, released on Thursday evening, which also requires stablecoin issuers to build the technical ability to freeze wallets, destroy tokens, and block transactions into their smart contracts.

item.title: Nigeria’s crypto firms face $744,000 capital rule as CBN, SEC divide oversight
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel Nwosu
item.description: The framework draws a clearer regulatory boundary for crypto businesses that combine trading with payments, requiring companies operating across both markets to secure authorisation from each regulator. It also raises compliance costs, prohibiting firms from counting the same capital toward their CBN and SEC requirements.
item.content:encoded:
Cryptocurrency companies licenced by Nigeria’s Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) will need separate central bank approval and at least ₦1 billion ($744,000) in additional capital to offer certain stablecoin payment, remittance, and custody services under new regulations.

The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) will oversee stablecoins used as payment instruments, transfers, foreign exchange (FX) conversion, and settlement. The SEC retains authority over crypto trading, investments, and digital assets classified as securities, according to new regulations released Thursday evening.

item.title: Habana went from World Cup winner to fintech beginner. Here’s what he learned.
item.dc:creator: Phathisani Moyo
item.description: When he stepped into the fintech boardroom, the skills that made him a rugby star did not automatically translate into business success.
item.content:encoded:
When PHATHISANI MOYO watched Bryan Habana deliver a presentation in Cape Town, he was intrigued by the personal journey to fintech behind one of South Africa’s most celebrated rugby careers.

Eight years after retiring from professional rugby, Bryan Habana found himself facing an unfamiliar opponent: himself.

The former Springbok winger and 2007 World Cup winner had spent much of his adult life mastering a sport that made him one of South Africa’s most recognisable athletes. He had represented his country on the biggest stage, performed under immense pressure and built a career around the discipline required to compete at the highest level.

But when he stepped into the fintech boardroom, the skills that made him a rugby star did not automatically translate into business success.
